source.title: Expert-Aware Refusal Steering
source.authors: Anna C. Marbut; Daniel R. Olson; Travis J. Wheeler

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies the original difference-in-means refusal-steering method to three MoE chat models and measures harmful-request attack success. It also decomposes steering into expert-level directions.
record.gate_note: The study reports direct ASR outcomes for ActAdd and expert-level steering. Direction-selection filter scores and routing statistics used to select or characterize experts are not included as rows here. Appendix A4 response-label distributions and routing comparisons are omitted because of the row limit.
record.test_reason: Applies Arditi et al.'s difference-in-means refusal direction, using their code, to three MoE chat models. It subtracts the direction and measures harmful-request ASR with a judge. This is the original method and measure in a new architecture. The expert-level decompositions measure where in the layer the signal sits, which is a localization question that matches no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors add that ActAdd works in MoE models, giving 65–95% ASR unimpeded by routing. A single expert recovers 78% of ActAdd ASR when free to choose its location, but only 54–61% when fixed to ActAdd's site, and less under safety prompts. They conclude that refusal is distributed unevenly rather than governed by one unified mechanism. They suggest system-prompt-driven refusal may sit in attention rather than the FFN experts.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation direction and subtracts it, as in the original method, but tests MoE models at selected layer/token locations rather than ablating the direction at every layer and position. Also decomposes directions into expert-specific outputs.
record.method_sensitivity: System prompt, model, intervention type, and whether expert steering can select its own layer and token position affect the reported recovery. Appendix D says steering coefficient effects are highly sensitive and non-monotonic.

fits_no_version.finding: Directions computed from expert outputs alone recover part of the ActAdd effect. Single expert, free location: 78% on average. Fixed at the ActAdd layer: 54–61%. Recovery is weaker under safety system prompts. The expert direction most similar to the ActAdd direction recovers about 60%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE models, the refusal direction is only partly computed by the FFN experts. Part of it comes from attention or the residual stream, especially under safety system prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Routing-defined safety experts do not predict effective steering directions. The routing difference shows little Spearman correlation with refusal score, and only OSS beats random selection (Tables 2–3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert routing differences between harmful and harmless prompts capture a different signal from the refusal steering direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Naively combining two expert directions on OSS drove ASR to 0–5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert-specific refusal directions do not combine additively.

record.problems: Small and medium open-source models only; the authors note limited compute. ASR is judged by GPT-4o, with 84.5% binary agreement with human raters. Intervention effects are sensitive to coefficient selection, and steering can produce non-responses and chain-of-thought leakage. No general capability evaluation is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Appendix A4 response-label distributions and the routing-statistics results in Tables 2–3 and Figures 3/A1, which are not the primary refusal-steering outcomes cataloged here. Also omitted detailed per-run location and coefficient settings in Table A5 and additional routing/cosine plots; the 57 retained rows prioritize intervention outcomes, partial effects, and condition differences.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts. Ablation at every layer and position, since only single-layer subtraction was tested. Preservation of general capabilities: no benchmark is reported, only a KL selection filter and non-response rates.
Whether refusal in the residual stream is affine, a cone, or multi-directional. Expert decompositions address localization, not dimensionality.
GPT-OSS 20B is a reasoning model, but reasoning was bypassed by forcing the final channel. Refusal after reasoning is not tested.
No analysis of other jailbreaks or adversarial training.
Only speculation, citing Lai et al. on detection vs. refusal experts. Nothing is measured.

record.verdict_notes: The 'not a single unified mechanism' conclusion concerns which sublayers compute the signal. It does not concern how many residual-stream directions refusal occupies, so it is not counted as V4 evidence. ActAdd ASR comes from a GPT-4o judge with 84.5% binary agreement with humans. ActAdd produced about 9–10% non-responses (Table A4), and capability preservation was not tested. OSS runs used 4-bit quantization and a forced final channel.

versions.untested_parts: Tests subtractive steering at a selected layer and token position, applied over prompt and generated tokens. Does not ablate the direction at every layer and position, test adding it to induce refusals on harmless requests, or establish that other abilities are largely intact.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
Does not test whether other jailbreaks suppress this direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Tests expert-level decompositions and one two-expert combination, but does not test affine or cone models of refusal.
The discussion proposes that routing may identify harmfulness detection while steering captures refusal control, but does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test.
No controlled comparison of refusal-training methods or training stages.
GPT-OSS 20B is a reasoning model, but the experiment forces its final channel rather than testing refusal after reasoning.

relation.reason: Its own Table 1 results (ActAdd ASR versus an unsteered baseline in three MoE models) bear directly on whether removing the direction removes refusal.

tranche.reason: Uses Arditi et al.'s code, difference-in-means direction and refusal/KL selection on Arditi splits, evaluated on 100 JailbreakBench harmful prompts. The intervention is the code's single-layer activation subtraction rather than all-layer ablation, and the judge is GPT-4o, so the recipe is close rather than exact.

source_check.notes: The text is arXiv:2606.04160v2, 'Decomposing Refusal Steering in Mixture-of-Experts Models' (Marbut, Wheeler, Olson, 2026), not 'Expert-Aware Refusal Steering'. It duplicates the 2606.04160 record, so count it once. GPT-OSS ran in 4-bit with reasoning bypassed (forced final channel), so V8 is not tested. ASR counts only full responses, judge self-consistency excluded ActAdd and baseline, and Table A4's OSS baseline (0.00) does not match Table 1 (0.10). The pack's verdicts carried no [lN] ids, so I numbered them l1 and l2 in listed order.

statements.correction: GPT-OSS 20B (4-bit), single-layer ActAdd subtraction, GPT-4o judge, 100 JailbreakBench prompts: ASR 0.94 (no prompt), 0.66 (lightweight), 0.83 (Llama-2), from baselines 0.10/0.00/0.00 (Table 1). Pooled over prompts, OSS ActAdd outputs are 0.81 full response, 0.09 refusal, 0.10 non-response (Table A4). The refusal rate per prompt setting is not given.
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but 0.66 is a full-response ASR from single-layer ActAdd subtraction, not a residual-refusal rate. The 0.34 shortfall mixes refusals and non-responses. The fuller Llama-2 safety prompt gives 0.83, so the drop does not grow with prompt strength.
